claim: Highest-impact work pairs a mostly conventional base with a small tail of unusual combinations; novelty without a conventional base does not pay.
note: One study (Uzzi 2013) cited four times. Foster 2015 (snippet only) is loosely consistent. Journal-pair novelty in citations is a proxy, not a test of reasoning quality.

claim: Distant recombination lowers the average outcome but raises variance, so both failures and breakthroughs come from unfamiliar search.
note: Fleming 2001, Wang et al. (2016 preprint and 2017 paper are one study), Foster 2015 (snippet). Citations are the outcome, so this is about science, not answers.

claim: Novel work is recognised late, so short-horizon scores undervalue it.
note: Only Wang, Veugelers, Stephan (preprint and published version). Counted once.

claim: LLM research ideas look more novel than expert ideas on paper but this edge disappears or reverses once ideas are executed.
note: All from the Si et al. study (2024 and 2025 follow-up, same team and pool). Preprint for the execution part.

claim: LLM novelty judgments are inflated: LLM ideas are often rewrites of prior work, judged novel by LLMs, and novelty scores relate negatively to later real impact.
note: Four independent preprints or experiments (novelty mirage, time-split study, Beel, Gupta and Pruthi, Domanti). Mostly preprints; two have no author list captured.

claim: LLM judges are near chance at ranking ideas and are biased by verbosity, so the generating model should not be the final selector.
note: Si 2024, Jiang 2025 hivemind, Domanti 2026, novelty mirage. Sycophancy adds a mechanism.

claim: Samples from one LLM, and across LLMs, are far more alike than human samples; repeated calls converge and aligned models lose diversity.
note: Si (5 percent unique of 4000), Doshi and Hauser RCT, Wenger and Kenett, Jiang, Padmakumar, Mohammadi, Anderson. Doshi lines b-06 and c-20 are one study. Directly supports our correlated-samples fact.

claim: LLMs rarely reach top human creativity levels per draw, but within-model variance is large, so many draws then selection raises the best result.
note: Haase 2025, Lu 2024, Tian 2024 (best-of-many 92.3 vs single-try 62.4). Preprints. Best-of-many needs a working selector, which is the judge claim.

claim: LLMs explore poorly and exploit poorly on their own; use the LLM to propose candidates and the program to track history, force untried options and pick.
note: Bandit and hidden-state tasks, not open-ended ideation. Krishnamurthy found GPT-4 explored well with chain of thought plus an external summarised history, which supports the program-run design. Transfer to idea search is by analogy.

claim: Without external feedback, LLM self-correction does not help and can hurt; critics tend to agree with the user's view (sycophancy).
note: Huang 2023 and Sharma 2023 are independent. Tension with our own result that always-doubt helped open tasks: see critique.

claim: Escalation of commitment is a robust, costly error that keeps losing paths alive.
note: One meta-analysis (Sleesman 2012). Human result; LLM analogue untested here.

claim: Small teams produce more disruptive work than large teams.
note: Wu et al. 2019 (snippet) versus critiques that the disruption index has data artefacts and bias (Holst 2024, Leibel and Bornmann 2023). Team-level, weak transfer.

claim: The disruption index and citation scores are not a clean machine-readable measure of breakthrough.
note: Holst 2024 (preprint) and Leibel and Bornmann 2023 review.

claim: Teams are more likely than solo authors to insert novel combinations into familiar knowledge.
note: Team only. Single agent analogue is weak because personas are correlated.

claim: Generating ideas alone first and pooling later beats interacting brainstorm groups.
note: Mullen 1991 meta-analysis and Girotra 2010. Both recorded from memory, not opened. Team-level; supports independent diverge calls then a separate selection step.

claim: Retrieving analogues from distant fields and recombining facets, or grounding in retrieved literature, gives ideas closer to real later research.
note: Three preprints with different methods. Effect sizes are small to moderate (about 7-10 percent similarity gain). Evaluation proxies are weak.

claim: Rewarding surprise (prior belief versus result) can steer search to more discoveries.
note: One benchmark paper, surprise measured by LLM beliefs.

claim: Divergent-then-convergent prompting with a feasibility reflection step raises efficient solutions on functional-fixedness problems.
note: Tian et al. 2024 only.

claim: Organisations under-invest in exploration because exploitation pays sooner; explicit explore and exploit budgets are needed.
note: March 1991 and its review, both snippet, organisation level. Individual-level evidence is thin.

claim: Problem finding (exploring and reframing before committing) predicts better creative work.
note: One art-student study (Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi 1976), snippet only; the intelligence claim rests on a review not opened.

claim: Evaluators penalise creative ideas under uncertainty, so novelty and usefulness should be rated on separate scales.
note: Mueller 2012, from memory. Human raters; LLM transfer untested.

claim: A portfolio of rare bets drives top impact (prize winners make more innovative moves).
note: Foster 2015, press coverage only.
